title: Reconstruct what someone did to this repository
summary: A colleague says 'I don't know, it just broke'. Read the reflogs to build a minute-by-minute timeline of every reset, rebase, checkout and merge they ran — then undo the damage.
mental_model: Git keeps a journal per ref: HEAD's own, plus one for every branch and remote-tracking ref. Together they record every pointer movement with a timestamp and the command that caused it. Nothing that moved a ref is invisible.

write.content:
IMPORTANT = 'three days of work'
MORE = 'and the tests'

steps.title: The symptom
steps.why: Two commits of work are missing from main and nobody knows where they went. `git log` cannot help — it only shows what is currently reachable.
steps.expect: No 'Add the important feature' commit anywhere in the visible history.

steps.title: Read HEAD's journal
steps.why: Every entry names the operation: commit, checkout, reset, merge. Read it bottom-up and you have the sequence of commands, in order, with the sha before and after each one.
steps.expect: A reset entry sitting in the middle — the moment the work left main.

steps.title: Read the branch's own journal
steps.why: `git reflog show main` covers only that branch, which cuts out the noise of checkouts between branches. Each branch and each remote-tracking ref has one of these.
steps.expect: A short list: three commits, a reset, a commit, a merge.

steps.title: Build the timeline with timestamps
steps.why: `--date=iso` and a format string turn the reflog into an incident timeline you can paste into a ticket. This is the artefact that ends the 'it just broke' conversation.
steps.expect: Each pointer movement, timestamped, with the command that caused it.

steps.title: Find the exact pre-reset commit
steps.why: `log -g` walks the reflog as if it were history, so you can search it by commit message — much easier than counting `HEAD@{n}` entries by eye.
steps.expect: The sha of the lost tip, recovered by searching the journal.

verify.label: the lost commit is findable in the reflog

steps.title: Recover the work onto a branch
steps.why: Give it a name and it stops being lost. Branching rather than resetting main means you can inspect the recovered work before deciding how to reintegrate it.

actions.run: sh -c 'git branch recovered/important $(git log -g --format=%H --grep="Test the important" -1)'

verify.label: the reset work is on a branch again

steps.title: Merge it back and record what happened
steps.why: Reintegrate deliberately with a merge, and write the incident down. The reflog is local and expires; a commit message is permanent and travels with the repository.

actions.run: git merge -q --no-ff -m "Merge recovered work that was lost to a reset --hard" recovered/important

write.content:
# Lost commits, recovered

Two commits were removed from main by a `git reset --hard HEAD~2`.
Found in the HEAD reflog and restored via a branch, then merged back.
Nothing was lost; the reflog would have expired after 90 days.

verify.label: the recovered work is back in the working tree
the commits destroyed by reset --hard are back on main
verify.hint: find them with git log -g, branch at that sha, then merge

verify.label: their content is in the working tree
the incident is documented in the repository, not just the reflog
the recovery branch is still there for reference

pitfalls: Reflogs are per-clone and never pushed. Forensics must happen on the machine where the commands were run.
Default expiry is 90 days for reachable entries and 30 for unreachable ones. After that, `git fsck --lost-found` is the only route left.
`git reflog` alone shows HEAD's journal. Branch-specific problems need `git reflog show <branch>`, which is a different list.
Reflog entries record the command name, not its arguments. A 'reset' entry tells you a reset happened, not what was typed.
`git log -g --grep` searches commit messages within the reflog — far easier than counting HEAD@{n} positions.
cheatsheet: walk the reflog as if it were history
find a lost commit by message
